When OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra on 3 September, the number that travelled was **99.9% on ARC-AGI-3**, set against GPT-5.6 Sol's 7.8% — and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang cited it three days later to declare that AGI had arrived. ARC Prize, the organisation that built the benchmark, published a different number on the same day: **62.7%**. Both are correct, and the distance between them is the most interesting measurement in AI right now.

## The Harness, Not the Weights

A harness is the scaffolding around a model: which tools it can reach, what it carries between requests, how context is compacted. Same weights, different scaffolding, different score.

ARC Prize ran Astra under its **standard harness** — a minimal, provider-neutral interface where the model decides which notes to keep — and got **62.7% at maximum reasoning, costing $26,098**. Under OpenAI's **Provider Adapter**, which preserves the model's opaque reasoning state across requests and compacts long conversations, it scored **99.9% for $18,817**. The better score was also the cheaper run.

The sharpest row in the table: set reasoning effort to *none* inside OpenAI's adapter and Astra still scores **96.7%** — 34 points above the same model at maximum reasoning inside the neutral harness. The scaffolding outperformed the reasoning dial outright. On the 167 game-reasoning pairs both harnesses solved, the adapter ran with **49% fewer tokens and roughly 3.66 times faster**.

## The Comparison That Wasn't Like-for-Like

Astra's 99.9% came from the adapter; Sol's 7.8% came from the standard harness. Those are different tests compared as if they were the same. The defensible number is **62.7% against 7.8%** — still an enormous jump, and still the top score on the benchmark.

ARC Prize declined the conclusion OpenAI drew: it stated plainly that it is "not claiming that it is AGI", with co-founder Mike Knoop writing that "we lack evidence to call this AGI yet". Going forward the foundation says it will publish both harness results side by side.

## The Numbers Kept Moving

Then the figures shifted. Fortune compared archived snapshots of OpenAI's launch post and found **five metrics altered** afterwards: Astra's hallucination rate read 4.2%, dropped to 2% by 5.20pm, then returned to 4.2%; Anthropic's Fable 5.1 fell nearly ten points on FrontierMath before settling at 83%; Sol's ExploitBench score doubled from 5.5% to 11.5%, with OpenAI now investigating a revert. The embargoed draft sent to media said 98.6% on ARC-AGI-3; the live post says 99.99%. OpenAI also pulled the post and put it back up, for reasons it would not disclose.

Stanford's Anka Reuel and Mike Hardy call the practice **benchmaxxing**. The deeper lesson is structural rather than moral: as scaffolds absorb more capability, the score stops describing the artifact being sold. If a benchmark is not run under a neutral harness for every lab — and both harness numbers published — the leaderboard measures who wrote the better adapter.
